newsitem.title: USA: Democratic Cuba would get billions of dollars - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Democratic Cuba would get billions of dollars - U.S..

text.p: A transition to democracy and capitalism in Cuba would attract billions of dollars in loans and investment, according to a U.S. government report due to be released this week.

"During a six year period following the establishment of a transition government, Cuba would receive from $4-8 billion from the international financial institutions, multilateral organizations and individual countries," a draft of the report obtained by Reuters said.
It said Cuba could also receive over one billion dollars anually from its expatriates in the United States, once Washington lifts restrictions on money transfers.

The report, largely based on political transitions in Eastern European countries, looks at how the United States would support the political and economic overhaul of the communist-ruled Caribbean island.
The White House is expected to issue the report on Tuesday or Wednesday to comply with the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act, better known as the Helms-Burton law.

Cuba is not a member of the International Monetary Fund or the World Bank. Nor can it trade with the United States, its closest neighbor, due to the U.S. embargo enforced since 1962 by Washington to weaken Cuban leader Fidel Castro.
The U.S. sanctions hardly hobbled Cuba while the Soviet Union was its main political and economic ally. But when Soviet communism crumbled in 1991, Cuba's economy plummeted.
Since then Castro has been trying to attract badly needed investment by opening up key economic sectors such as tourism, mining and telecommunications to foreign partners.
The Helms-Burton law tightens the U.S. embargo by trying to deter investment on the island by threatening to punish foreign firms benefiting from property seized under Castro.
President Bill Clinton signed the law in March, shortly after Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two small planes flown by Cuban exiles based in Miami, killing four of them.

But faced with mounting opposition to the measure from U.S. allies, Clinton has postponed a controversial provision allowing U.S. citizens, including naturalized Cuban exiles, to sue foreigners investing in their confiscated properties.
The Helms-Burton law establishes conditions for the United States to recognize a transitional government in Cuba, mainly that Castro no longer be in power.

The new report details what Cuba has to gain by moving towards democracy and calling free elections. "Economic sanctions will be suspended and negotiations will be initiated to promote bilateral trade relations," it said.
In a clear message to the Cuban military, the report said Washington would be ready to cooperate with Cuba's armed forces if they backed a civilian democratic government and respected human rights.
It said the United States would be prepared to negotiate with a transitional government the return of the Guantanamo naval base at the southeastern end of the island.

"Although the Cuban armed forces constitute one of the most important pillars of the present regime, they could potentially play a positive role in Cuba's transition," it said. "The militaries in other former communist countries have acquiesced or actually assisted in democratic transitions."
